claim: Hfq is an RNA chaperone protein in bacteria.
source: As one of the most abundant RBPs in bacterial cells, Hfq is an important and prevalent post-transcriptional gene regulator (Brennan and Link, 2007; Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states that Hfq is an important post-transcriptional gene regulator in bacterial cells, with supporting citations.

claim: Hfq protects small RNAs (sRNAs) from degradation.
source: Acting as a chaperone of sRNA-mediated gene regulation, Hfq protects small RNAs (sRNAs) from degradation and promotes sRNA–mRNA duplex formation (Brennan and Link, 2007; Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: The text explicitly states this function with supporting citations.

claim: Hfq promotes sRNA–mRNA duplex formation.
source: Acting as a chaperone of sRNA-mediated gene regulation, Hfq protects small RNAs (sRNAs) from degradation and promotes sRNA–mRNA duplex formation (Brennan and Link, 2007; Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: The text explicitly states this function with supporting citations.

claim: Binding of sRNAs to target mRNAs leads to changes in the translation activity and stability of the mRNAs.
source: Binding of sRNAs to target mRNAs further leads to changes in the translation activity and the stability of the mRNAs (Storz et al., 2011; Wagner and Romby, 2015).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with supporting citations.

claim: Loss of Hfq compromises the fitness of bacterial cells, especially under harsh conditions.
source: Loss of Hfq compromises the fitness of bacterial cells, especially under harsh conditions, and abolishes the virulence of bacterial pathogens (Sobrero and Valverde, 2012; Tsui et al., 1994).
evidence: The text explicitly states this with supporting citations.

claim: Loss of Hfq abolishes the virulence of bacterial pathogens.
